source.title: On the Shortness of Life
source.attribution: Seneca, On the Shortness of Life (trans. Aubrey Stewart), Standard Ebooks, public domain
source.notes: Taken from Seneca, Dialogues (trans. Aubrey Stewart), Standard Ebooks.

cards.title: Life isn't too short; we spend too much of it carelessly
cards.body:
Seneca rejects the common complaint that life is cruelly brief. We are given enough time to do important things, he argues, if we arrange it well. The real problem is leakage: hours drained by distraction, indulgence and drifting without purpose.

The point stings because it puts the issue back in our hands. A year can feel like nothing when it's spent on autopilot, or rich when it's aimed at a few things that matter.
cards.quote: We do not have a very short time assigned to us, but we lose a great deal of it: life is long enough to carry out the most important projects
cards.apply_it: Look at yesterday honestly. Estimate how many hours went to things you'd choose again, and how many simply leaked away.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, I ¶1

quiz.question: What was Seneca's main claim about the length of life?
options: Life is far too short to achieve anything
Only the rich have enough time
Life is long enough if we use it well
quiz.explanation: He argued we are not given a short life; we make it short by wasting it.

cards.title: Guard your time at least as fiercely as you guard your money
cards.body:
Seneca marvels at a contradiction. People fight over a strip of land or refuse to hand out cash, yet let anyone walk in and take their hours. We are stingy with property and wildly generous with the one thing we can never earn back.

The modern version is the calendar invite accepted without thought, the meeting with no agenda, the call that could be an email. Saying no to a time request is not rude. It protects your most limited resource.
cards.quote: You cannot find anyone who wants to distribute his money; yet among how many people does everyone distribute his life?
cards.apply_it: Before accepting the next request for your time, ask: would I pay money for this? If not, decline or shorten it.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, III ¶1

quiz.question: What contradiction did Seneca point out?
options: People guard their property but give away their time freely
People save time but waste money
People work too little and rest too much
People value friends more than family
quiz.explanation: We protect money and land jealously but let others encroach on our lives.

cards.title: A divided mind can't let anything take root
cards.body:
Seneca noticed that nothing, whether eloquence or learning, can be done properly by someone whose attention is elsewhere. A distracted mind rejects whatever you try to put into it, the way hard ground rejects seeds.

It's an old observation about multitasking. Reading with notifications pinging or listening while drafting a reply produces shallow results. If you want something to stick, give it your whole attention for a stretch, even a short one.
cards.quote: nothing, neither eloquence nor literature, can be done properly by one who is occupied with something else; for nothing can take deep root in a mind which is directed to some other subject, and which rejects whatever you try to stuff into it.
cards.apply_it: Pick one task today and do it for 25 minutes with your phone in another room. Notice how much more sticks.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, VII ¶1

quiz.question: Why did Seneca say a busy, distracted person cannot learn well?
options: Because learning is only for the young
Because nothing takes deep root in a mind directed elsewhere
quiz.explanation: A mind occupied with other things rejects what you try to plant in it.

cards.title: Postponing life until later is the biggest waste of it
cards.body:
People work hard now so they can live well someday: after the promotion, after retirement, after the kids leave. Seneca calls this planning for life at the expense of life itself. Waiting steals today by promising something better tomorrow, and tomorrow isn't guaranteed.

You can still plan. But build the things you value into this week instead of parking them in an imagined future: the walk, the call to a friend, the project you care about.
cards.quote: postponement is the greatest waste of life: it wrings day after day from us, and takes away the present by promising something hereafter … everything future is uncertain: live now straightaway.
cards.apply_it: Name one thing you've been saving for "when life calms down". Put a small version of it in your calendar this week.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, IX ¶1

quiz.question: What did Seneca call the greatest waste of life?
quiz.explanation: Postponement takes away the present by promising something hereafter.

cards.title: Free time spent fretting or fussing is not real rest
cards.body:
Seneca observed that some people's leisure is busy. Alone at home, they still worry, tinker and obsess over trivial things, so their downtime is just another kind of work.

A weekend spent refreshing the news, tweaking a hobby setup or replaying the work week isn't rest, even if no one's paying you. Real leisure leaves you clearer and calmer. It may mean doing less, or doing one absorbing thing fully, instead of keeping your mind on a low boil.
cards.quote: Some men’s leisure is busy: in their country house or on their couch, in complete solitude, even though they have retired from all men’s society, they still continue to worry themselves: we ought not to say that such men’s life is one of leisure, but their very business is sloth.
cards.apply_it: Plan one hour of true rest this week: no screens, no chores, no planning. Notice whether you feel restored afterwards.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XII ¶1

quiz.question: What did Seneca mean by "busy leisure"?
options: Free time still filled with worry and trivial fussing
quiz.explanation: He described people who retire from society yet keep worrying, so their idleness is a kind of busyness.

cards.title: Forgetting the past, ignoring the present and fearing the future shrinks life
cards.body:
Seneca describes the people whose lives feel shortest: they don't learn from what's behind them, they skim past the present, and they dread what's ahead. Each habit removes a slice of the only life they have.

The remedy is a better relationship with all three. Look back to learn and appreciate. Live the present with attention. Plan for the future without letting fear run it. A life held this way feels longer, not because it is, but because it's actually lived.
cards.quote: Those men lead the shortest and unhappiest lives who forget the past, neglect the present, and dread the future
cards.apply_it: Tonight, take two minutes: one thing you learned from the past, one moment you enjoyed today, one worry you can set aside.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XVI ¶1

quiz.question: Which three habits did Seneca say make for the shortest lives?
options: Forgetting the past, neglecting the present, dreading the future
Working, eating and sleeping too much
quiz.explanation: Those habits waste all three parts of time.

cards.title: Without a settled purpose, you'll drift from scheme to scheme
cards.body:
Seneca lists the many ways people let life slip away: endless greed, pointless busyness, drink, laziness, chasing other people's approval. One group he singles out is those with no settled aim, who jump from one new plan to the next out of restlessness, never finishing anything.

A clear purpose doesn't have to be grand. It just gives you a way to say yes or no to opportunities. Without it, every new idea looks equally urgent, and years pass in constant starting over.
cards.quote: a great number have no settled purpose, and are tossed from one new scheme to another by a rambling, inconsistent, dissatisfied, fickle habit of mind
cards.apply_it: Write one sentence describing what you want this year to be about. Use it to judge the next new opportunity that tempts you.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, II ¶1

quiz.question: What happens to people with no settled purpose, according to Seneca?
options: They are tossed from one new scheme to another
quiz.explanation: Without a fixed aim, a restless mind keeps switching plans and achieves little.

cards.title: Make an appointment with yourself
cards.body:
Seneca notices that ambitious people complain bitterly when an important person won't see them. Yet they never give themselves a hearing. They are busy defending, pleading for and serving others; nobody, he says, belongs to himself.

The important person will eventually grant you a meeting. But will you ever sit down with yourself, listen to your own worries and think about your own life? Time alone to reflect is not selfish; it's how you notice whether you're living the life you actually want.
cards.quote: no one lays claim to his own self, everyone wastes his time over someone else.
cards.apply_it: Block 20 minutes in your calendar this week labelled 'Me'. Spend it alone, without a phone, thinking about how your life is going.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, II ¶3

quiz.question: What does Seneca say busy people never do?
quiz.explanation: They seek audiences with others but never make time to listen to themselves.

cards.title: Audit where your years actually went
cards.body:
Seneca imagines asking a very old man to tally his life on paper: how much time went to creditors, quarrels, running errands for others, illness brought on by himself, idle hours, useless grief and polite chit-chat. Subtract all that, and he would find he had lived far fewer years than his age suggests.

You can do a smaller version of this exercise. Track a normal week honestly. The result is often surprising, and it shows exactly where to reclaim time for the things you say matter most.
cards.quote: Come now, reckon up your whole life in black and white
cards.apply_it: For one normal day, note what you did each hour. At the end, circle the hours that truly mattered to you.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, III ¶1

quiz.question: What would the old man discover by tallying his life, according to Seneca?
options: He had used every hour wisely
He had lived fewer real years than he counted
He had spent too much time alone
He was younger than he thought
quiz.explanation: After subtracting wasted time, he'd see he had not lived as many years as he counted.

cards.title: Even the most powerful long for rest; success alone won't give it
cards.body:
Seneca points to the Emperor Augustus, who had more power and blessings than anyone of his age. Yet he constantly wished he could put down his duties and live for himself, and he found comfort just in imagining that future leisure.

It's a striking reminder that getting to the top doesn't automatically bring peace. If the most powerful man in the world dreamed of rest, it's worth building some of that freedom into your life now, rather than assuming it will arrive with the next promotion.
cards.quote: He thought leisure so important, that though he could not actually enjoy it, yet he did so by anticipation and by thinking about it.
cards.apply_it: What 'someday' rest are you waiting for? Find one small piece of it you can enjoy this week instead.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, IV ¶1

quiz.question: What did Augustus long for despite his power?
options: Leisure and rest from his duties
quiz.explanation: Even the most powerful man dreamed of laying aside his greatness to rest.

cards.title: Complaining about your busy life changes nothing
cards.body:
Seneca describes powerful men who, while others envied them, privately hated how they had spent their years. Yet their complaints changed nothing: once they had vented, they went straight back to the same habits.

Many of us do the same, moaning about overwork, stress or lack of time, then saying yes to the next obligation. Complaining can feel like doing something about the problem, but it isn't. If something genuinely bothers you, choose one concrete change and make it.
cards.quote: yet by these complaints they have effected no alteration either in others or in themselves: for after these words have escaped them their feelings revert to their accustomed frame.
cards.apply_it: Pick the complaint you repeat most about your schedule. Replace it with one specific action you'll take this week.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, VI ¶1

quiz.question: What did the powerful men's complaints achieve, according to Seneca?
options: No change in others or in themselves
quiz.explanation: After venting, they slipped back into the same habits.

cards.title: Learning how to live takes a whole lifetime
cards.body:
Seneca notes that most skills can be learned quickly, some even by children who then teach others. But how to live well has no quick course. It takes a whole lifetime, and even many great people die admitting they haven't fully worked it out.

This isn't discouraging; it's liberating. You don't need to have life figured out by 25, 40 or 60. Treat living well as a skill you keep practising, with room to grow at every age.
cards.quote: but one’s whole life must be spent in learning how to live, and, which may perhaps surprise you more, one’s whole life must be spent in learning how to die.
cards.apply_it: Write down one lesson about living well you've learned in the past year, and one you're still working on.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, VII ¶1

quiz.question: How long does Seneca say it takes to learn how to live?
options: It can't be learned at all
quiz.explanation: Seneca says one's whole life must be spent learning how to live.

cards.title: Being alive a long time isn't the same as living long
cards.body:
Grey hair and wrinkles, Seneca says, don't prove someone has lived long. A person who spent decades tossed about by other people's demands has merely existed for a long time. He compares it to a ship caught by storms just outside the harbour, blown round and round in the same spot: it hasn't voyaged far, it has only been tossed about.

The question isn't how many years you'll have, but how many of them you'll actually live with intention.
cards.quote: such a man has not lived long, but has only been long alive.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: if this past year were a voyage, did I travel somewhere, or just get tossed around? Choose one direction for next month.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, VII ¶1

quiz.question: What image does Seneca use for someone who has merely been long alive?
options: A ship tossed around near harbour by storms
A traveller who visits many lands
quiz.explanation: Such a person hasn't travelled far; they have only been tossed about.

cards.title: Plan your days as if you were planning your life
cards.body:
Seneca observes that most people hurry through life, longing for the future and bored with the present: 'When will this year be over? When will the holidays come?' In contrast, the person who uses all their time for their own chosen purposes, arranging each day as if it were the plan of their life, neither craves nor fears tomorrow.

Each day is a small model of your whole life. If your days are filled with what matters to you, the years will be too.
cards.quote: but he who disposes of all his time for his own purposes, who arranges all his days as though he were arranging the plan of his life, neither wishes for nor fears the morrow
cards.apply_it: Tonight, plan tomorrow around one thing that matters to your life's direction, not just your to-do list.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, VII ¶1

quiz.question: How does Seneca describe the person who arranges each day like a life plan?
options: They are always longing for holidays
They are the busiest people in the city
They neither wish for nor fear tomorrow
quiz.explanation: Someone who lives each day by their own purpose doesn't crave or dread the future.

cards.title: When someone asks for your time, notice what you're really giving
cards.body:
Seneca is amazed at how freely people ask for each other's time, and how willingly it's given. Both sides think about what the time is for, but neither thinks about the time itself, as if it cost nothing. Because time is invisible, we treat it as cheap, yet the same people would give everything to live longer when facing death.

Next time someone asks for 'just a quick call' or 'five minutes', remember you're spending something you can never get back. It's fine to give it, but give it deliberately.
cards.quote: both parties consider the object for which the time is given, but neither of them thinks of the time itself
cards.apply_it: Before agreeing to the next meeting or favour, pause and ask: is this worth an hour of my life? Then decide.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, VIII ¶1

quiz.question: Why does Seneca say people waste time so freely?
options: Because they have plenty of it
Because others pay them for it
Because time can be recovered later
Because time is invisible, so it seems cheap
quiz.explanation: Time is incorporeal and unseen, so people value it very little until it's running out.

cards.title: Life won't warn you how fast it is passing
cards.body:
Seneca describes time as moving silently. It doesn't make noise, doesn't slow down at a king's command, and never turns back. Nobody will return your years to you. And while you're busy, life hurries on regardless.

Because there's no alarm bell, it's easy to assume there's always more time. That's why Seneca urges us to pay attention now. Notice the years passing, not with fear, but with the awareness that makes today worth using well.
cards.quote: It will make no disturbance, it will give you no warning of how fast it flies: it will move silently on
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you keep meaning to call or visit. Do it this week, without waiting for a reason.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, VIII ¶1

quiz.question: How does Seneca describe the passing of life?
options: It moves silently and gives no warning
It slows down when we are busy
It can be extended by powerful people
quiz.explanation: Life passes silently; it never warns us or stops for anyone.

cards.title: Use your time as quickly as it slips away
cards.body:
Seneca quotes a poet who said the best days of a mortal's life are the first to fly. His response: since time moves fast, our use of it must move just as fast. Treat it like a rushing stream that won't flow forever, and drink from it while you can.

This isn't a call to frantic busyness. It's a call to stop delaying what matters: the course you want to take, the conversation you keep postponing, the project you plan to start 'when things calm down'. Things rarely calm down.
cards.quote: Our swiftness in making use of our time ought therefore to vie with the swiftness of time itself, and we ought to drink of it as we should of a fast-running torrent which will not be always running.
cards.apply_it: Name one meaningful thing you've postponed 'until later'. Take the first small step on it today.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, IX ¶3

quiz.question: What image does Seneca use for how we should use time?
options: Storing water in a deep well
quiz.explanation: Since time flows quickly and won't last, we should use it as eagerly as drinking from a torrent.

cards.title: Busy people reach old age before they notice it coming
cards.body:
Seneca compares life to a journey. Travellers absorbed in conversation, reading or thought often arrive at their destination before realising they were close. In the same way, people who are always busy suddenly find themselves old, unprepared, never having noticed it creeping up day by day.

The cure is to look up now and then: to ask where you are, where you're going, and whether you're ready for the next stage. Pausing to notice the journey makes the arrival less of a shock.
cards.quote: so in this fast and never-ceasing journey of life, which we make at the same pace whether we are asleep or awake, busy people never notice that they are moving till they are at the end of it.
cards.apply_it: On your next birthday or New Year, write a short note on where you are in life and what you want the next five years to hold.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, IX ¶3

quiz.question: Why do busy people reach old age unprepared, according to Seneca?
options: They never notice they're moving until the end
quiz.explanation: Like distracted travellers, busy people don't notice life's journey until it's nearly over.

cards.title: Live so that you can enjoy looking back
cards.body:
Seneca divides life into past, present and future. The present is brief and the future uncertain, but the past is fixed: nothing can take it from you. Yet busy people avoid looking back, because their memories are full of regret: greed, cruelty, deceit or waste.

The lesson works in two directions. Take time to review your past calmly, since it is a secure part of your life. And act today in a way you'll be glad to remember, so that looking back becomes a source of strength rather than shame.
cards.quote: must needs fear his own memory; yet this is a holy and consecrated part of our time, beyond the reach of all human accidents
cards.apply_it: Before bed, recall one moment from today you'll be glad to remember. Tomorrow, try to create another.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, X ¶1

quiz.question: Why does Seneca call the past a precious part of our time?
options: It can be changed if we try
It is the shortest part of life
It is fixed and can't be taken away
quiz.explanation: The past is beyond Fortune's reach; but only a clear conscience lets us enjoy revisiting it.

cards.title: Don't wait for a crisis to change how you spend your life
cards.body:
Seneca describes people who, only when illness reminds them they're mortal, suddenly confess they've been fools and haven't really lived. They promise that if they recover, they'll spend the rest of their days differently, and realise how much they've toiled for things they never enjoyed.

Many people have this moment after a health scare, a death in the family or a close call. Seneca's challenge is to have that realisation now, while you're well, so that your priorities change by choice, not by emergency.
cards.quote: they reflect how uselessly they have laboured to provide themselves with what they have never enjoyed, and how all their toil has gone for nothing
cards.apply_it: Imagine you've just had a health scare. What would you promise to change? Pick one item and start it this week.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XI ¶1

quiz.question: When do the people Seneca describes finally realise they haven't really lived?
options: When illness reminds them they are mortal
quiz.explanation: A brush with mortality makes them see their toil was for things they never enjoyed.

cards.title: Ask of what you learn: will it make me any better?
cards.body:
Seneca pokes fun at people who spend their time on trivia, like how many rowers Ulysses had, or which Roman general first did this or that. Such facts don't make you wiser in private and only make you tiresome in public.

His test is simple: whose mistakes will this knowledge reduce? Whose passions will it calm? Who will it make braver or fairer? Curiosity is good, but with limited time it's worth favouring learning that actually improves how you live, work and treat people.
cards.quote: whose mistakes will be made fewer by such stories? whose passions will be restrained? whom will they make more brave, more just, or more gentlemanly?
cards.apply_it: Look at the last three things you read or watched. Which one will change how you act? Choose more like that this week.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XIII ¶1

quiz.question: What test does Seneca apply to knowledge?
options: Is it rare and hard to find?
Does it make anyone wiser, braver or more just?
quiz.explanation: Seneca values learning that reduces mistakes and improves character, not idle trivia.

cards.title: Reading great thinkers adds their centuries to your life
cards.body:
Seneca says the people who truly have leisure are those who spend time with the great thinkers of the past. They don't just live their own years; they borrow the whole history of human wisdom. You can argue with Socrates, doubt with the sceptics, or rest with Epicurus.

Today that access is easier than ever: libraries, free e-books, podcasts and translations bring the best minds of every era within reach. A few pages a day lets you learn from lifetimes of experience you could never live yourself.
cards.quote: we may argue with Socrates, doubt with Carneades, repose with Epicurus, overcome human nature with the Stoics, exceed it with the Cynics.
cards.apply_it: Choose one classic book (free online if needed) and read ten pages a day for a week.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XIV ¶1

quiz.question: Why does Seneca say students of philosophy 'alone really live'?
options: They gain the wisdom of all past ages
quiz.explanation: By studying great thinkers, they add all the centuries before them to their own life.

cards.title: You can't choose your parents, but you can choose your mentors
cards.body:
We don't get to pick the family we're born into, Seneca says, but we can choose which 'family' of great minds we adopt. Pick the thinkers you want to belong to, and you inherit not just their name but their wisdom, which grows larger the more it's shared.

These mentors are never too busy, never flatter you, and will tell you the truth without insult. Whether through books, teachers or role models, choosing whose ideas you absorb is one of the most powerful decisions you make about who you'll become.
cards.quote: We are wont to say that we are not able to choose who our parents should be, but that they were assigned to us by chance; yet we may be born just as we please
cards.apply_it: Name two thinkers, writers or elders whose way of living you admire. Find one piece of their wisdom to read or hear this week.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XV ¶1

quiz.question: What does Seneca say we can choose, even though we can't choose our parents?
options: Which family of great minds we adopt
quiz.explanation: By choosing which thinkers to follow, we can in a sense choose the family we belong to.

cards.title: Remember the past, use the present, prepare for the future
cards.body:
Seneca describes the wise person's life as long because they make use of all three kinds of time. They recall the past through memory, use the present fully, and look ahead to the future with preparation rather than fear.

Most of us lean on just one: dwelling on old regrets, getting lost in today's busyness, or worrying about tomorrow. A rich life draws on all three. Learn from what's behind you, act on what's in front of you, and plan calmly for what's ahead.
cards.quote: If any time be past, he recalls it by his memory; if it be present, he uses it; if it be future, he anticipates it: his life is a long one because he concentrates all times into it.
cards.apply_it: Take five minutes today: one lesson from your past, one thing to do now, one step to prepare for next month.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XV ¶1

quiz.question: Why is the wise man's life 'a long one', according to Seneca?
options: He makes use of past, present and future
He lives only in the present
He worries constantly about the future
quiz.explanation: He gathers all three kinds of time into his life: memory, use and anticipation.

cards.title: Some prizes cost more to keep than they did to win
cards.body:
Seneca observes that great success is often enjoyed with fear. The higher something rises on luck, the further it can fall. People work very hard to gain wealth or status, then work even harder and more anxiously to hold on to it.

That doesn't mean ambition is wrong. But before chasing a bigger house, title or lifestyle, it's worth asking: what will it cost to maintain? A modest life you can sustain calmly may be richer than a grand one you must guard day and night.
cards.quote: very wretched, therefore, as well as very short must be the lives of those who work very hard to gain what they must work even harder to keep
cards.apply_it: Before your next big purchase or goal, write down what it will cost to maintain in money, time and worry.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XVII ¶1

quiz.question: What does Seneca say about people who win great prosperity?
options: They can finally relax for good
They must work even harder to keep it, and live in fear
They become more generous with time
quiz.explanation: Much of what we gain by great effort must then be guarded anxiously.

cards.title: Each goal reached can just become the next source of stress
cards.body:
Seneca notices a pattern: people finish one ambition and immediately start another. One hope leads to the next, one job to another. They don't look for an end to their stress; they just change what it's about. Leisure is always wished for and never enjoyed.

It's worth asking whether your goals have a finish line. If every achievement simply opens a new demand, decide in advance what 'enough' looks like, and allow yourself to enjoy it when you get there.
cards.quote: they do not seek for an end to their wretchedness, but they change its subject.
cards.apply_it: Pick one current goal and write down what 'enough' looks like. When you reach it, celebrate before setting a new one.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XVII ¶1

quiz.question: What does Seneca say ambitious people do after reaching one goal?
options: Change the subject of their worries to a new goal
quiz.explanation: They don't end their stress; they just transfer it to a new ambition.

cards.title: Knowing your own mind matters more than mastering your job
cards.body:
Seneca writes to his friend Paulinus, who managed Rome's grain supply with great skill and honesty. Seneca praises him, but urges him to make time for himself too. He reminds Paulinus that his education was meant for something greater than counting grain shipments.

The point applies to anyone whose job absorbs them. Professional skill is valuable, but understanding yourself, what you value and how you want to live, is the foundation that everything else rests on.
cards.quote: yet, believe me, it is better to understand your own mind than to understand the corn-market.
cards.apply_it: Set aside time this weekend to write answers to: What do I value most? Is my daily life reflecting that?
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XVIII ¶1

quiz.question: What did Seneca tell Paulinus is better than understanding the corn-market?
quiz.explanation: Seneca urged his friend to value self-knowledge above even excellent professional work.

cards.title: Measure your life by how much of it is truly yours
cards.body:
Seneca says the unhappiest busy people are those who don't even work on their own affairs. They sleep when another sleeps, walk at another's pace, and even love and hate on someone else's orders. If they want to know how short their life is, he says, they should count how small a part of it belongs to them.

Most of us must work for others. But it's worth guarding some time that's fully yours, spent on choices you make, with people you choose, for reasons that are your own.
cards.quote: If such men wish to know how short their lives are, let them think how small a fraction of them is their own.
cards.apply_it: Estimate how many hours last week were truly your own choice. Find one way to add an hour next week.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XIX ¶1

quiz.question: How does Seneca suggest busy people measure the shortness of their lives?
options: By how small a fraction of it is their own
By comparing their wealth with others
By how many offices they've held
quiz.explanation: The more of our time is controlled by others, the shorter our real life is.

cards.title: Don't envy people with impressive titles; they paid with their years
cards.body:
When you see someone constantly in the spotlight, wearing the robes of high office, Seneca says, don't envy them. They gained it by giving up huge parts of their life. Some throw away years chasing one prestigious position; some die before reaching it; others endure endless indignities only to get an inscription on their tombstone.

Before wishing for someone else's status, ask what it actually cost them in time, health and relationships. You may find you wouldn't pay that price.
cards.quote: When, therefore, you see a man often wear the purple robes of office, and hear his name often repeated in the forum, do not envy him: he gains these things by losing so much of his life.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone whose position you envy. List what they likely gave up to get it. Would you trade?
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XX ¶1

quiz.question: Why does Seneca say not to envy someone who holds high office?
options: They gained it by losing much of their life
High office is easy to get

cards.title: Learn to stop working before work stops you
cards.body:
Seneca tells of Turannius, a meticulous official in his nineties who, when relieved of his duties, had his household mourn him as if dead until his job was given back. Seneca notes many people cling to work longer than they're able, seeing old age as bad only because it sets them aside.

The law may let you retire, he says, but you have more trouble giving yourself permission. Having interests, friendships and a sense of self beyond your job makes stepping back, at any age, a beginning rather than a loss.
cards.quote: men have more difficulty in obtaining their own consent than that of the law to a life of leisure.
cards.apply_it: Name one interest or relationship outside work that you'd want to grow if you had more time. Give it an hour this week.
cards.locator: On the Shortness of Life, XX ¶1

quiz.question: What did Turannius do when relieved of his duties?
options: Had his household mourn him as if he were dead
quiz.explanation: He was so attached to work that losing it felt like death to him.
